headline: India approves first dengue vaccine for people aged 4 to 60
summary: The health ministry has authorized the use of Takeda's Qdenga jab, which protects against all four dengue virus serotypes.
details: India's Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) has approved the Japanese drugmaker Takeda's Qdenga vaccine for individuals between 4 and 60 years of age.
The vaccine protects against all four dengue virus serotypes and has already been approved in 42 countries, including the UK, Switzerland, and the European Union.
According to the health ministry, over 24 million doses have been distributed worldwide with no major safety concerns reported so far.
Takeda is collaborating with Indian vaccine maker Biological E to expand the manufacturing of the drug within the country.
The move comes as dengue cases have exploded globally due to rising temperatures, urbanization, and changing weather patterns.
The WHO reports that nearly half the world's population is at risk, with an estimated 100 million to 400 million infections annually.
Since 2021, India has reported over one million dengue cases and at least 1,500 deaths, according to official data.
India is also developing its own vaccine, DengiAll by Panacea Biotec, which is currently in final-stage clinical trials and may become a single-dose option.
caption:
India has officially approved its first dengue vaccine. The jab is authorized for people aged 4 to 60.

India's Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) has approved the Japanese drugmaker Takeda's Qdenga vaccine for individuals between 4 and 60 years of age.

The vaccine protects against all four dengue virus serotypes and has already been approved in 42 countries, including the UK, Switzerland, and the European Union.

According to the health ministry, over 24 million doses have been distributed worldwide with no major safety concerns reported so far.

Takeda is collaborating with Indian vaccine maker Biological E to expand the manufacturing of the drug within the country.

The move comes as dengue cases have exploded globally due to rising temperatures, urbanization, and changing weather patterns.

The WHO reports that nearly half the world's population is at risk, with an estimated 100 million to 400 million infections annually.

Since 2021, India has reported over one million dengue cases and at least 1,500 deaths, according to official data.

India is also developing its own vaccine, DengiAll by Panacea Biotec, which is currently in final-stage clinical trials and may become a single-dose option.

headline_marked: Houthis [[impose naval blockade on Saudi Arabia]], opening new front in US-Iran war
headline: Houthis impose naval blockade on Saudi Arabia, opening new front in US-Iran war
summary: The move threatens global energy supplies and trade, as Iran's President Pezeshkian declares a 'full-scale war' with the United States.
details: Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis have declared a maritime embargo against Saudi Arabia, citing an 'eye for an eye' response to a Saudi-led siege on Yemen.
The blockade opens a new front in the ongoing conflict between the US and Iran, widening the threat to global energy supplies and trade beyond the Gulf region.
Full closure of the Bab el-Mandeb gateway to the Red Sea could cut global oil supply by 7 percent, adding to existing disruptions that have already reduced shipments by 10 percent.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has stated that his country is in a 'full-scale war' with the United States and must accept the repercussions.
The conflict has escalated with US strikes on Iranian cities and IRGC attacks on US military assets in Jordan, Syria, Kuwait, and Bahrain.
The IRGC reported that two oil tankers exploded in the strait, while another vessel was struck by a unknown projectile off the coast of Oman.
Despite the military escalation, mediators have proposed a 10-day ceasefire to salvage an interim deal and end the war that began on February 28.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has vowed that the US will continue to target Iran as long as it attacks global commercial shipping.
caption:
A new front opens in the US-Iran war as Houthis impose a naval blockade on Saudi Arabia, threatening 7% of global oil supply.

Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis have declared a maritime embargo against Saudi Arabia, citing an 'eye for an eye' response to a Saudi-led siege on Yemen.

The blockade opens a new front in the ongoing conflict between the US and Iran, widening the threat to global energy supplies and trade beyond the Gulf region.

Full closure of the Bab el-Mandeb gateway to the Red Sea could cut global oil supply by 7 percent, adding to existing disruptions that have already reduced shipments by 10 percent.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has stated that his country is in a 'full-scale war' with the United States and must accept the repercussions.

The conflict has escalated with US strikes on Iranian cities and IRGC attacks on US military assets in Jordan, Syria, Kuwait, and Bahrain.

The IRGC reported that two oil tankers exploded in the strait, while another vessel was struck by a unknown projectile off the coast of Oman.

Despite the military escalation, mediators have proposed a 10-day ceasefire to salvage an interim deal and end the war that began on February 28.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has vowed that the US will continue to target Iran as long as it attacks global commercial shipping.
